description: This is a course about how money works, not about what to buy. It is written for a student on an allowance, a fresh graduate reading a first payslip, a VA or freelancer whose income is different every month, and anyone who sends money home before paying their own bills. lessons.content_mdx:
# What you actually earn

Mika accepted a job at ₱18,000 a month. Her first payslip came, the money landed in her account, and it was smaller than that. Nobody stole anything and payroll made no mistake. She had been planning her life around the wrong number.

None of this is advice about your own money: it is the mechanism, so take the specifics to the source that applies to you.

## Gross is the headline, net is the money

Gross pay is the figure in the offer letter. Net pay, sometimes printed as take-home, is what survives everything listed in between. Rent, fare, the money you send home and anything you manage to keep are all paid out of net. A plan built on gross is a plan for money you never touch.

So the first skill in this course is unglamorous: read a payslip top to bottom and name every line on it.

## The three kinds of deduction

**Mandatory contributions.** SSS, PhilHealth and Pag-IBIG come off before you see the money. They are not fees for nothing. Each one makes you a member of an arrangement with benefits attached, including sickness and maternity benefits, hospital coverage, and a fund you can borrow against or put toward a home. The rates and the ceilings are set by law and they change. Get the current ones from SSS, PhilHealth and Pag-IBIG themselves, and do not trust a figure quoted anywhere else, this course included.

**Withholding tax.** Your employer estimates the income tax you owe and remits it in slices, payday by payday. It is easy to believe you pay no income tax when you have never watched it leave. How it is computed is BIR's to publish, not a course's to summarise.

**Whatever your employer deducts on top.** A salary advance you took mid-month. An SSS or Pag-IBIG member loan you are repaying. Late minutes and absences. Coop dues, a uniform, tools you were issued.

That third group is the one to check every payday, because it is where a mistake actually shows up. If a line carries a label you cannot explain, ask payroll what it is. Asking once is a normal question. Paying it for a year without asking is expensive.

Two job offers are only comparable at the net line. The gap between two headline salaries and the gap between two take-home figures are different numbers, and the second one is what you live on.

## 13th month pay is not a bonus

Thirteenth month pay is required by law for covered rank-and-file employees. It is not a reward a manager grants, and a hard year for the company does not make it optional. DOLE publishes who is covered and how it is computed, and that is where to settle your own case rather than in a group chat. Anything handed out on top of it is a separate bonus, and that one really is discretionary.

The risk with 13th month pay is not that it fails to arrive. It is that it arrives without a name on it. Money with no name gets spent, and by the second week of January all that is left is the memory of a good December. Decide before it lands what each part is for. January is not a surprise: the tuition instalment, the fare back after the holidays and the annual renewals all sit on dates you already know.

## When there is no payroll behind you

If you are a VA, a freelancer, or anyone paid per project or per shift, almost none of the machinery above runs for you. It depends on who is paying you. A Philippine company engaging you as a contractor or professional is generally required to withhold a share of your fee and hand you a certificate for it, and that certificate is money: you credit it against your own tax later, so ask for it rather than assuming it does not exist. An overseas client withholds nothing and files nothing. Either way, nobody is computing your contributions or filing your returns for you.

The money is still not all yours. Income tax is owed on it. SSS, PhilHealth and Pag-IBIG all have arrangements for self-employed and voluntary members, which means the contributions are yours to make rather than yours to skip, and the member benefits only exist if you are a member. The difficulty is not arithmetic, it is psychological: ₱46,000 sitting in your account looks exactly like ₱46,000 you are free to spend.

The fix is mechanical. Split it the day it arrives. A set share moves into a separate account you do not spend from, and only the rest gets budgeted. What that share should be, how to register, which forms and which deadlines apply to you: take those to BIR or to an accountant who can see your actual situation.

## Before the next lesson

Read your most recent payslip line by line, out loud. If you are freelance, open your last client payment and write down two figures: what arrived, and what share of it was never yours to spend.

lessons.title: The month you can describe
lessons.content_mdx:
# The month you can describe

Ask anyone where their money goes and you get a story. Rent, food, load, fare, and then it is gone. The story is short, tidy and light by a few thousand pesos, because a story is a memory, and memory rounds every small spend down to nothing.

You cannot budget a story. You can budget a month you can describe.

## Track the month you are actually in

The instinct is to wait for a normal month and track that one. Do not wait. Track the month you are in, fiesta and hospital visit and broken charger included, because a normal month is a thing you invent afterwards to explain why the money ran out.

One month is enough to start. You are not building an accounting system. You are collecting evidence.

## How to do it without an app

Any of these works, and the one you will actually keep doing is the right one.

- A note on your phone. One line per spend: amount, what it was, how you paid.
- A notebook by the door, filled in when you get home.
- Every receipt into one pocket of your bag, emptied and added up on Sunday night.

Four rules make it survive the week:

- Log it the same day. By tomorrow it is already a story.
- Include the small ones. The ₱20 spends are the entire reason you are doing this.
- Count everything that left you, not just cash: e-wallet transfers, card taps, money you sent someone, load bought for your mother.
- Do not judge while you log. Judging while logging is how people quietly stop logging.

Ten minutes on Sunday to add up the week. Ten more at the end of the month.

## Then sort it into two piles

**Fixed costs** were decided once and now arrive whether or not you think about them: room rent, a tuition instalment, an internet plan, a postpaid line, a loan repayment, an insurance premium.

**Variable costs** are decided again every single day: food, fare, load, delivery, drinks, gifts, the pasalubong.

The difference matters because the two piles are changed in completely different ways. A fixed cost changes only when you make one deliberate decision: move, downgrade, renegotiate, cancel. That is rare, it takes an afternoon, and it is worth doing when the number is big.

A variable cost changes through small choices you make while tired. That is the pile where a month is won or lost, and it is the pile that never appears in the story you tell about your money.

## The leaks that never feel like decisions

Look for these in your month, because they hide well:

- **Load and data.** Bought in small amounts, whenever it runs out, so it never registers as a bill. Add the month up. That total is the bill.
- **Delivery.** The meal costs more than the menu says, once every line at checkout is added on top of the food. Compare a delivered meal with the same food bought downstairs and you will see the real price of being tired.
- **Silent renewals.** Streaming, music, storage, a game pass, a design tool you used once for a client. Open your card or e-wallet history for the last three months, list every charge that repeats, and cancel anything you cannot immediately name.
- **The daily small one.** Coffee and pandesal every morning. The milk tea after shift. Nobody is telling you to stop. You just have to know that it is a monthly number, not a daily one.
- **Sige, ako na.** The rounds you pay for, the fare you cover, the gift you go halves on and then quietly go three quarters on.

## The number at the end

At the end of the month, write three figures: what came in, what went out, and the gap between them.

If more went out than came in, the difference was filled by something real. Savings you had. A loan. A relative. A bill you did not pay. Name which one, because that thing is now part of next month too.

You now know something you did not know four weeks ago. You can finish this sentence with numbers instead of a shrug: last month I earned about this, I spent about that, and the largest thing I did not expect to see was this.

That sentence is what the next lesson turns into a budget.

lessons.title: A budget for an income that moves
lessons.content_mdx:
# A budget for an income that moves

Jhen does admin work for three clients from a bedroom in Iloilo. One pays on the first, one pays when the invoice is a week old, and one pays whenever someone in another country remembers. The budgeting advice she keeps reading assumes money lands on the fifteenth and the thirtieth. Hers does not.

That advice is not wrong. It was written for a salary, and it breaks in one specific place: it assumes the amount arriving is the amount you can plan against.

## Budget from a low month

Put your last six months of income in a row. Jhen's look like this: ₱42,000, ₱18,000, ₱31,000, ₱27,000, ₱12,000, ₱35,000.

The average is about ₱27,500. Do not build on the average. The average is a month that never actually happened, and it quietly promises that a good month will cover a bad one, which is only true if you make it true.

Build on the low ones instead. Jhen's lowest month was ₱12,000. That is the figure her fixed costs have to fit inside. If they do not fit, the gap is the first thing to fix, by moving a fixed cost down or by holding enough back in the good months to cover it before it arrives. Everything she earns above that line is not spending money. It is next month's salary, arriving early.

## Pay yourself

Set it up like a payroll, with you as both the company and the employee.

Client payments all land in one account. That account is a holding pen, not a wallet. On a fixed date, you move one set amount from it into the account you actually spend from. That transfer is your salary, and it is the same figure whether the month was fat or thin.

A fat month refills the holding account. A thin month draws it down. The pile in between is your buffer, and its whole job is to make the date and the amount boring.

Start smaller than feels satisfying. In the first months there is barely a buffer and you pay yourself out of what is there. That is normal, not a failure. How large the buffer should get, and why it outranks everything else you could do with money, is the whole of the next chapter.

## Two piles you are not allowed to touch

The tax and contribution share from lesson one comes out first, on the day the money arrives, into an account you do not spend from.

Then separate the business from the person. A client payment is not your income. It is revenue, and out of it come your internet, your software, your load, your fare, your equipment fund and the tax share. What is left is what the business can afford to pay you. Same trick as gross and net, run by you instead of an HR department.

## The costs that arrive once a year

Tuition instalments. Insurance renewals. A permit renewal. Christmas. These have dates on them and you know the dates.

Divide each one by the number of months until it is due and set that aside monthly. Skip this and a known cost turns up dressed as an emergency, and gets paid for with borrowed money, which means paying more for exactly the same thing. Chapter 2 turns that extra into a number you can compare.

## Money you send home is a line, not a leftover

If you support people, decide the amount in advance, put it in the plan next to rent, and send it on the same date every month.

Sending whatever is left at the end does two things you do not want. It teaches everyone at home to wait and then ask, which puts the negotiation in the worst possible week. And it makes your best month look like your new normal, so the next request is sized against a month you cannot repeat.

Say the number out loud to them. "I can send this much on the tenth" is a harder sentence than silence, and it is the one that lets your family plan too. If it has to change, say so before the date rather than after.

## The test

You understand your money when you can explain it to another person in under a minute, without opening anything.

"In a low month I take in about this. My fixed costs are that. I pay myself this amount on the fifth. This much goes home on the tenth. This much never gets touched because it is tax. Anything above that stays in the holding account."

If you cannot say it, you do not have a budget yet. You have a hope.

Your specific tax, your specific contributions and your specific debts belong with BIR, with the agency itself, or with a licensed professional you have checked. What this course hands you is the mechanism.

quiz.prompt: Mika accepted an offer of ₱18,000 a month. Her first payslip shows ₱18,000 at the top, a column of deductions under it, and a smaller figure at the bottom that matches what reached her bank. She is sure she has been shortchanged. What is actually going on?

options.text: The company is holding back part of her pay while she is on probation, and will release the difference once she is regular.
Payroll has set its own deductions on her salary, so she can ask them to lift the charges until she is settled in the job.
The ₱18,000 is gross pay. Mandatory contributions and withholding tax come out of it, and the bottom figure is her net.
A first payslip runs short when the cut-off lands mid-month, so the missing amount will correct itself on the next payday.

quiz.explanation: Gross is the offer, net is the money. Between them sit mandatory contributions to SSS, PhilHealth and Pag-IBIG, withholding tax that your employer remits for you, and anything the employer deducts on top such as a salary advance or a member loan. None of that is optional and none of it is a mistake. A probationary salary is not held back in part and released later, and a payslip that covers a short first cut-off says so on its period line rather than leaving you to guess at it. What Mika should do is name every line, and ask payroll about any line she cannot name. For the current rates and ceilings, the agencies themselves are the only source worth trusting.

quiz.prompt: Arvin's 13th month pay lands in the second week of December. Last year it arrived and by mid-January he could not say where it had gone. He knows his sister's tuition instalment falls in January and that his phone is dying. What makes the difference this year?

options.text: Treat it as the year's reward and let it carry Christmas, then deal with the January costs out of the January salary.
Wait until it lands before deciding anything, since the exact amount is not certain until payroll has computed it.
Decide now what each part of it is for, write the amounts down, and move every one of them on the day that it lands.
Put the whole thing into the household budget in December and see what is still there when January starts.

quiz.explanation: Thirteenth month pay is required by law for covered rank-and-file employees, so it is not a bonus anyone decides to grant. DOLE is where to check who is covered and how it is computed. The danger is not that it fails to arrive, it is that it arrives with no name attached, and money with no name gets spent. Tuition dates and January fares are known in advance, which makes them budget lines rather than surprises.

quiz.prompt: Rina tracked every peso for a month. A fiesta, a wedding gift and a replacement laptop charger all landed in the same four weeks, and the total shocked her. She decides to throw the month out and track a quiet one instead, so she gets a clean baseline. What does that decision cost her?

options.text: It costs her four weeks. A quiet month gives her the same figures without three one-off costs distorting the total.
Nothing much. She can keep the total, take the three one-off costs out of it, and treat what is left as her monthly figure.
Only time. She should track two more months first, then plan against the average of the three so no single one distorts it.
It costs her the truth about her year: other months bring the same kind of cost under another name, so a quiet baseline breaks on a loud month.

quiz.explanation: There is no typical month, there are only months where the irregular cost has a different name: a fiesta, a hospital visit, a birthday, a repair. Waiting four weeks for a quiet one buys her a cleaner-looking number and a budget that works right up until real life shows up. Subtracting the one-offs and averaging three months are both better than throwing the evidence away, but they hide the same thing, which is that irregular costs deserve a line of their own.

quiz.prompt: Dennis logs a month and shows you the list: room rent, an internet plan with months left on the contract, a Pag-IBIG loan repayment taken off his pay, and ₱2,400 spent across the month on food delivery during late shifts. He says he cannot cut anything because it is all fixed. Which part of that is not fixed?

options.text: The rent. It is the largest number on the list, so it is where any saving worth the effort would have to come from.
The delivery. He chose it again on each of those late shifts, and it is the line his own daily decisions move.
The loan repayment. It is taken off before he ever sees the money, so it never got the chance to be part of a plan.
The internet plan. He signed it before the late shifts started, so it no longer matches the way he actually lives now.

quiz.explanation: A fixed cost was agreed once and changes only through one deliberate decision: moving, downgrading, renegotiating, cancelling. Rent and the internet plan can change that way, but not this week and not by trying harder. The delivery total was assembled from a dozen separate choices made while tired, which is exactly what makes it the line he can move now. Fixed does not mean permanent, it means it is not this month's argument.

quiz.prompt: Jhen has six months of freelance income behind her: ₱39,000, ₱21,000, ₱30,000, ₱14,000, ₱25,000 and ₱33,000. She wants a monthly plan she will not have to abandon in the first bad month. Which figure should her fixed costs fit inside?

options.text: About ₱14,000, her lowest month, with everything she earns above it going into the account she pays herself from.
About ₱27,000, the average of the six, since the strong months and the weak ones cancel each other out over a year.
About ₱21,000, her second-lowest month, on the basis that ₱14,000 was an unusually bad month that will not repeat.
About ₱33,000, her most recent month, because her rate has gone up and the older figures no longer describe her work.

quiz.explanation: An average is a month that never happened, and planning against it means the thin months are funded by borrowing or by not paying something. Her lowest month is the figure her fixed costs have to fit inside: everything above that line goes into the holding account, so a strong month is what pays her during a weak one. If they do not fit inside ₱14,000, the gap is the first thing to fix, by moving a fixed cost down or by holding enough back in the good months to cover it. Treating the worst month as a one-off is how a plan survives exactly until the next one.

quiz.prompt: A client payment of ₱46,000 lands in Jhen's account. The client is overseas, so nothing was withheld, there is no payslip, and nobody is filing anything on her behalf. What should she do on the day it arrives?

options.text: Keep it in one account and track in her head what part is owed, so the whole balance stays available if a client pays late.
Budget the full amount now and pay what is owed later out of whatever she happens to be earning when the deadline arrives.
Treat it as clear income, since nothing was deducted from it and no employer filed anything for her this month.
Move a set share into a separate account she does not spend from, and take the rates, forms and deadlines to an accountant.

quiz.explanation: An employee's tax and contributions leave before the money is ever visible. A freelancer's do not, so the money looks spendable for weeks before the bill exists. Splitting it on arrival is the only version of this that survives a slow month. Tracking it in your head fails the first time a client pays late. What share to set aside, how to register and which deadlines apply are questions for BIR or an accountant who can see her actual situation.

quiz.prompt: A strong month leaves Jhen with ₱20,000 still sitting there after her fixed costs, the salary she paid herself, and the money she sent home. Two of her clients have gone quiet, so next month already looks thin. What is that money for first?

options.text: Sending more home this month, since the household is stretched and a strong month is exactly what should be carrying it.
Staying in the account she pays herself from, so that a thin month still pays her the same amount on the same date.
A separate savings goal for the laptop she will need when her current one gives up, which is coming one way or another.
Paying some of next month's fixed costs early where a provider takes it, so a thin month has fewer bills waiting inside it.

quiz.explanation: On an income that moves, the first job of a surplus is to make your own pay predictable: a fat month funding a thin one is the entire point of the holding account. Sending more home is real generosity and the laptop is a real cost, but both are safer once your salary is not in question. Paying bills early is not wrong, it just converts flexible money into money you can no longer redirect. How large this buffer should get, and why it comes before anything else, is the next chapter.

quiz.prompt: Rina's tuition instalment of ₱9,000 is due Friday. A client paid late, she has ₱3,500, and a lending app on her phone will send the difference today. The instalment date has been on the school's schedule since June. What is the move?

options.text: Ask the school what its options are on the date she is short, and start setting the instalment aside monthly from this month on.
Borrow the ₱5,500 from the app. The amount is small, the money arrives today, and one instalment is not worth losing a semester over.
Cut what she sends home this month and quietly make it up next month, so the tuition gets covered without any borrowing at all.
Wait until Friday in case the client pays, then decide on the day whether the app or the family is the better route to take.

quiz.explanation: The date was published in June, which makes this a fixed cost that could have been funded in monthly pieces, not an emergency. Borrowing for a cost you knew about means paying more for the same tuition, and chapter two turns that into a figure you can compare. Cutting the money home without saying so moves the shortfall onto people who never agreed to carry it. Waiting until Friday just removes the options you still have today.

lessons.title: The buffer comes first
lessons.content_mdx:
# The buffer comes first

Aileen does transcription for two clients in Cebu. In March her laptop screen went black in the middle of a deadline. She had nothing set aside, so she borrowed ₱12,000 from an app that released ₱10,800 into her wallet and wanted ₱12,000 back in a month. She kept the clients. She could not find ₱12,000 in thirty days, so she borrowed again to cover it, and then again. Four months later the laptop was long since fixed and she was still paying for it.

That is the whole argument for an emergency fund, and it has nothing to do with being cautious. Without money set aside, a surprise becomes a loan, at whatever price is available on the day you are desperate. The buffer is not the opposite of investing. It is what stops your emergencies from costing more than any return you were hoping to earn.

A buffer is money set aside for shocks, kept where you can reach it within a day or two, that you do not touch for anything else. It is there so the next black screen is an annoying week instead of a four month debt.

## Size it against your own spending

You will be handed round numbers. ₱100,000. Six months. A year of expenses. None of them was calculated from your life.

Your fund replaces spending, not income. Start from the number you found when you tracked a real month: rent or your share of it, food, transport, load and data, the contributions you owe, whatever you send home.

Say Rhea's ordinary month comes to ₱14,000. One month of cover is ₱14,000. Three months is ₱42,000. Now she has a target that means something, and she can say out loud why it is that number.

How many months is a judgement call, and the honest input is how fast your income could come back. An employee on a steady payroll sits differently from a freelancer whose two clients could both go quiet in the same week. Irregular income needs a deeper buffer, for the same reason a banca carries more fuel when the weather is unpredictable.

Nobody builds a full target in one go. ₱14,000 saved is already a month you do not have to borrow for.

## What counts as an emergency

Three tests. It was not planned, it will not wait, and not dealing with it costs you more than dealing with it.

Enrollment is not an emergency. You have known the date since last year. Neither is a sale, a trip your barkada organised, or a phone that still works. Those are expenses, and expenses belong in a budget line.

A hospital admission is an emergency. So is the laptop, if the laptop is how you earn. Write your own version of that list before you need it, because the moment you need it is the moment everything feels urgent.

## Boring, reachable, and slightly awkward

- **Boring.** The amount should not move. A fund whose value can fall is not a fund, because emergencies do not wait for it to recover.
- **Reachable.** You should be able to get at it within a day or two. Money locked away for five years is not a buffer, whatever it earns.
- **Slightly awkward.** Not in the account you pay for load and lunch from. Separate it enough that spending it takes a decision.

Where you keep it belongs to the next chapter.

## Yes, it loses buying power. Keep it anyway

Prices rise over time, so money that sits still buys less each year than it did. That is inflation, and it is the word anyone selling you something will reach for. It is a fair argument against holding a mountain of idle cash. It is not an argument against holding a buffer. It is an argument for sizing one against your own spending. The fund is insurance, and what it buys is the ability to say no to a lender.

## Spending it is not failure

Mark had ₱30,000 set aside and spent ₱22,000 of it on his father's hospital bill. He told himself he was back to zero. He was not. He was ₱22,000 better off than the version of him who would have borrowed that bill. The fund did the exact thing it existed to do, and refilling it goes back to being an ordinary line in the budget.

## Say your own number

Say your buffer target out loud, as a number, with the reason attached. "My month costs about ₱14,000, I want three months because my income is irregular, so my target is ₱42,000 and I am at ₱9,000." Nobody else gets to set that number for you.

lessons.content_mdx:
# What compounding actually does

Quick note before the mechanism: this lesson names no product and recommends none, on purpose.

## What a return is

What you get back beyond what you put in. You put in ₱10,000, a year later you have ₱10,400, and the ₱400 is the return. It can come from interest paid on money you lend, a share of a business's profit, or rent from something you own. It can also be negative, which is a sentence a sales pitch will never say out loud.

## Compounding is returns earning returns

Pick a number so the arithmetic is easy. Say ₱10,000 grows by 10 percent in a year. That figure is invented for the sake of the sum. It is not a prediction, not an offer, and not a rate anyone is promising you.

Year one: ₱10,000 becomes ₱11,000. You earned ₱1,000.

Year two: the 10 percent is applied to ₱11,000, not to the original ₱10,000, so you earn ₱1,100 and end with ₱12,100.

Year three: ₱13,310.

That extra ₱100 in year two is the entire idea. Your money earned money, and then that money went to work too. The difference does not stay small, because each year starts from a bigger number than the last, and none of it asks you to do anything except leave it alone.

## Time is the input you cannot buy back

Trina is 22 and can set aside ₱1,500 a month. She is thinking of waiting five years until her salary is bigger, because ₱1,500 feels too small to bother with.

What she gives up is not the ₱90,000 she would have put in, which a bigger salary could replace later. What she cannot get back is five years of growth earning its own growth, because that only happens by money sitting there while time passes.

Money you add later still works. It just has fewer years to do it in. Time is the only input in this lesson that is not for sale, which is why starting small and early is not a consolation prize.

## Risk and return travel together

Nobody hands out extra return for free. If an arrangement offers you more, it is paying you to carry something: the chance the business fails, the chance the borrower does not repay, the chance you need the money on the exact day its value is down.

That is not a warning, it is how the pricing works. A higher promised return means somebody decided you are being paid to accept a bigger chance of loss, and that chance does not disappear because the person explaining it is confident.

Two related ideas, one sentence each, because this course does not teach you to pick anything. **Spreading**, which a salesperson will call diversification: putting everything into one company, one scheme or one friend's venture means a single bad outcome takes all of it. **Fees and lock-ins**: a fee comes out of your money whether or not there was a return that year, and a lock-in means the money is not yours when you need it, which is why the buffer from the last lesson stays separate from anything locked.

## The sentence that carries into the next chapter

Nobody can guarantee a return, because nobody controls what the money earns.

That is not cynicism, it is the same logic as everything above. A return comes from an outcome in the world: a business trading, a borrower repaying, a price moving. The person offering you the deal controls none of those, so a promise of a fixed high return every month is a promise about something outside the promiser's power. Either the return is not guaranteed, or the money is not being earned the way they say.

Deposits and government arrangements work differently, and the next chapter deals with where your money sits and who stands behind it. Keep the sentence anyway. When somebody says guaranteed, they have told you something about themselves.

## It runs the other way too

All of this works identically when you are the one who owes. Interest charged on a balance that already includes last month's interest grows against you exactly as fast as it would have grown for you. That is the next lesson.

## The two questions to ask

You can now explain why ₱1,000 left alone for ten years is not the same as ₱1,000 held for one year, ten times over. And you can ask anyone selling you an investment the two questions that matter: what has to happen for this to pay, and what happens to my money if it does not?

lessons.title: What a loan really costs
lessons.content_mdx:
# What a loan really costs

Every borrowing offer you will ever be shown can be turned into one number: how many pesos leave your hands, in total, over a year.

Not the rate. Not the monthly payment. The pesos. Lenders quote rates and payments because those numbers make an offer sound small. That is not the number you need.

## Count everything, not only the interest

The cost of a loan is everything you hand over minus everything you receive:

- interest, however it is described
- processing, service or documentation charges
- anything deducted before the money reaches you
- an insurance or protection charge added to the loan
- late penalties, if you are honest about the chance of being late

That third line is the one that catches people. Dexter needs ₱15,000. An app approves ₱15,000, deducts a ₱1,200 service charge, and sends ₱13,800 to his wallet. In 30 days he owes ₱15,000. He borrowed ₱13,800 and paid ₱1,200 for it, and if he takes the same loan again each month to cover the last one, that is ₱1,200 twelve times in a year, ₱14,400 on a line of money that was never bigger than ₱13,800.

Set that beside a member loan through an employer or a government fund, where the same ₱15,000 is repaid over twelve months and the total he hands over comes to ₱16,100. That is ₱1,100 for the year. Same borrower, same amount, wildly different price.

Those numbers are invented so the arithmetic is visible. Real offers vary; the method does not.

## A rate quoted per week or per day hides its own size

Three percent sounds like nothing. Three percent a week is fifty two of those in a year. Half a percent a day is a different animal again.

When a rate arrives attached to a short period, count how many of that period fit into a year, then work out the pesos. Not an annual percentage, but the only question that matters: if this runs for a year, how much have I paid?

## 5-6, and being fair about it

The name is the deal: you borrow five and pay back six over an agreed stretch, collected daily.

Nanay Cely borrows ₱5,000 at the palengke and repays ₱150 a day for 40 days, which is ₱6,000. That loan cost her ₱1,000. She takes a new one the day the old one closes, so that is roughly nine cycles in a year and about ₱9,000 paid on a line of money never larger than ₱5,000. Those are the numbers in this example. Terms differ from lender to lender, so run the arithmetic on the offer in front of you.

Be fair about why she uses it. There is no form, no requirement, no waiting, and the money is in her hand within the hour. A formal lender may cost far less and be no use at all if the money arrives in two weeks. She is paying for speed, and it is worth naming that instead of pretending she is being foolish.

What she can do is know the price. Once you can say "this speed costs me around ₱9,000 a year", you can decide whether it is worth it, and start moving toward a buffer that makes the next cycle unnecessary. That is a decision. Not knowing is not.

## Interest on the original, or interest on what you still owe

This is the distinction that explains why two loans quoting the same rate can cost different amounts.

Vince is offered ₱24,000 over twelve months at "one percent a month" by two lenders.

**Lender A charges on the original amount.** One percent of ₱24,000 is ₱240, every month, for twelve months. Total interest: ₱2,880. How much he has already repaid makes no difference.

**Lender B charges on the remaining balance.** Month one, he is charged on ₱24,000. Month two, on what is left. By month ten he is charged on a small balance and pays very little interest, so his total lands well below Lender A's on the identical quoted rate.

Add it up. Say Vince repays ₱2,000 of the principal each month. He is charged on ₱24,000, then ₱22,000, then ₱20,000, and so on down to ₱2,000 in the final month. Those twelve balances total ₱156,000, and one percent of that is ₱1,560 against Lender A's ₱2,880. Same quoted rate, and Lender B's interest comes to a little over half of Lender A's.

The words to listen for are flat, add on, or "computed on the principal" for the first, and diminishing or declining balance for the second. If nobody will tell you which it is, ask for the total amount payable.

## Four questions, before you sign anything

1. How much money actually reaches me?
2. How much do I hand over in total, and by when?
3. Is the interest on the original amount or on what I still owe?
4. What happens if I am late, in pesos?

Get the answers in writing. A lender who will not put the total payable on paper has told you something about the total.

## What you can now do

Take any two offers, work out what each costs in pesos over a year, and say which is cheaper and by how much. Nothing else is needed to compare them honestly.

quiz.prompt: Rhea's ordinary month costs her about ₱14,000. A friend tells her the standard emergency fund is ₱100,000 and that she should aim for that. What is the sensible way for Rhea to set her target?

options.text: Use the ₱100,000, since a round figure from a common rule is easier to commit to and to check herself against.
Save whatever is left over at the end of each month, with no target at all, until the balance feels like enough.
Multiply her own ₱14,000 month by however many months of cover she wants, and treat that figure as the target.
Size it against her monthly income instead, since her income is the thing an emergency actually interrupts.

quiz.explanation: A buffer replaces spending, and it replaces yours rather than somebody else's. Starting from Rhea's own ₱14,000 gives her a target she can explain and check: three months of cover is ₱42,000. The ₱100,000 was calculated from nobody's life. Saving with no target is how a fund quietly turns into spending money, and sizing against income overshoots for anyone who earns more than they spend.

quiz.prompt: Kier needs ₱10,000 for six months. Lender A charges a flat 2 percent a month on the ₱10,000 and no fees. Lender B charges 1.5 percent a month on the ₱10,000 but deducts an ₱800 processing fee before releasing the money. Which is cheaper?

options.text: A is cheaper: A costs ₱1,200 in total, while B's ₱900 of interest plus the ₱800 fee comes to ₱1,700.
B is cheaper, because its monthly rate is the lower of the two and the rate is what a loan costs you.
B is cheaper, because a processing fee is a one-time charge and is not part of the cost of the borrowing.
They land in roughly the same place, once B's ₱800 fee is spread across the six months of the loan.

quiz.explanation: Cost is everything you hand over minus everything you receive. B's interest is ₱900, but ₱800 never reached Kier, so B costs him ₱1,700 on ₱9,200 received. A costs ₱1,200 on the full ₱10,000. The lower rate lost. Spreading the fee over the months changes how it feels and not what it totals.

quiz.prompt: Bong, who works your shift, put ₱50,000 into a group that pays him ₱5,000 every month. He has been paid for a year, shows you the screenshots, says the return is guaranteed, and mentions he gets a bonus if he signs you up. What does that guarantee actually tell you?

options.text: That the returns are real, since Bong has been paid every month for a year and can show you each one.
That the risk is low, because a fixed payout means the money is not exposed to a market that moves.
That you should put in a small amount you can afford to lose, and watch closely what happens to it.
That nobody can promise a return, because nobody controls what the money is supposed to be earning.

quiz.explanation: A return comes from an outcome in the world: a business trading, a borrower repaying, a price moving. Whoever is offering the deal controls none of those, so a guaranteed monthly figure is a promise about something outside their power. Bong being paid proves that somebody paid him and nothing else, and a reward for recruiting you is a reason to ask where that payout money comes from. A small test amount is what the structure needs from you, not a way to check it.

quiz.prompt: Mark had ₱30,000 set aside and spent ₱22,000 of it on his father's hospital admission. He is now at ₱8,000, feels he wasted a year of saving, and is thinking of putting future savings somewhere that grows instead. What is the right read?

options.text: He should leave the ₱8,000 where it is and send everything he saves from now on somewhere that grows.
The fund did exactly its job, and refilling it is the ordinary next step rather than a punishment.
He should borrow the ₱22,000 to restore the fund to ₱30,000, and then repay that loan slowly.
He should treat ₱8,000 as his new target, since a fund that size only invites him to spend it.

quiz.explanation: Spending a buffer on the exact thing it was built for is the fund working, not failing. Mark is ₱22,000 better off than the version of him who would have borrowed that bill at whatever price was available that night. Refilling goes back to being an ordinary line in his budget. Borrowing to refill defeats the point, and shrinking the target to whatever survived leaves him short at the next admission.

quiz.prompt: Nanay Cely borrows ₱5,000 from a lender at the palengke and repays ₱150 a day for 40 days. She takes a new one the day the old one closes. Her cooperative has offered her a loan she would repay monthly instead. What comparison should she run?

options.text: Add up what each one costs her in pesos over a full year of borrowing, and set the two totals side by side.
Compare the ₱150 a day she pays now against the monthly payment the cooperative would want from her.
Stay with the daily one, since small daily amounts out of the day's takings are easier for her to keep up with.
Compare the two quoted rates against each other, since the charge is small on either side of it.

quiz.explanation: Her cycle costs ₱1,000 and repeats roughly nine times over a year, so the honest figure is about ₱9,000 on a line of money never larger than ₱5,000. Only a pesos-per-year total makes two differently shaped loans comparable. Setting a daily payment beside a monthly one compares nothing, and a rate quoted over a short period hides its own size. The speed she is paying for may still be worth it to her, but she should know the price before she decides.

quiz.prompt: Marco receives ₱18,000 of 13th month pay. He has nothing set aside, a ₱6,000 balance on a lending app that costs him heavily every month, and a friend inviting him into an investment with a three-year lock-in. What should he do with it?

options.text: Put all of it into the investment, since a lump sum like this is the only chance he really gets to start.
Split it evenly between the debt, a buffer and the investment, so that all three of them move at once.
Hold back a small starter buffer, clear the lending app balance with the rest, and leave the lock-in well alone.
Leave it in the spending account, so that all of it is there if something comes up during the month ahead.

quiz.explanation: A small buffer comes first so that the next surprise does not go straight back onto the same app, and then clearing an expensive debt is the one return he knows he will get, because the cost stops the day the balance does. Investing while that balance runs is paying a high certain price to chase an uncertain gain, and a three-year lock-in puts the money out of reach exactly when a surprise arrives. Splitting evenly feels balanced and leaves the most expensive thing running. Money parked in a spending account is money already half spent.

quiz.prompt: Vince is offered ₱24,000 over twelve months at one percent a month by two lenders. One computes the interest on the original ₱24,000 every month, the other on the balance that is left. The totals come out different. Why?

options.text: Because the second lender collects its charge at the end of the term rather than at the start of it.
Because the first charges on ₱24,000 all year, while the amount he actually owes keeps falling.
Because a rate quoted monthly and a rate quoted yearly are counted in two different ways here.
Because the second one spreads the very same total interest across a larger number of payments.

quiz.explanation: On the original amount, one percent of ₱24,000 is ₱240 every month for twelve months, or ₱2,880, including the final month when Vince owes almost nothing. On a declining balance he is charged on what is actually outstanding, and that shrinks every month, so his total lands well below ₱2,880. Listen for flat or add-on against diminishing or declining balance, and if nobody will say which it is, ask for the total amount payable.

quiz.prompt: Trina is 22 and can set aside ₱1,500 a month. She plans to wait five years until her salary is bigger, because ₱1,500 feels too small to be worth starting with. What is she actually giving up?

options.text: Nothing much, since a larger amount started five years later covers exactly the same ground.
The ₱90,000 of contributions, which a bigger salary later on can comfortably catch up on.
Time in the market, which she can buy back later by accepting a higher level of risk.
Five years of growth earning its own growth, which is the one input she cannot redo later.

quiz.explanation: A larger amount started later does not cover the same ground: the returns those five years would have earned are themselves earning by the time she finally begins. The ₱90,000 is the part she can replace, since a bigger salary later can put that in. What she cannot replace is five years of any return also earning a return, because that only happens by money sitting there while time passes. Accepting more risk later is not the same thing either, since risk buys a wider range of outcomes rather than extra years.
