lessons.title: How the scams are built
lessons.content_mdx:
# How the scams are built

Ask anyone who ever put money into one of these schemes how they heard about it, and the answer is almost never a stranger. It is a cousin, a workmate, someone from the old batch group chat, holding real screenshots of a real payout. That detail is the whole trick. The proof is genuine. It is genuine proof of the wrong thing.

## One engine, several costumes

The schemes built for students, VAs and jobseekers share a mechanism: the money paid to early members is money that later members put in. Nothing is being produced or sold. That is why payouts continue only while new people keep joining, why bringing in friends is rewarded, and why every message carries a deadline. When recruitment slows, the payouts stop, and the people left holding the loss are the ones who joined last and put in the most.

Whoever showed you their receipt was very likely paid honestly, with money that came from whoever joined after them. If you join, you become the source of the next receipt they forward.

Chapter 2 ended on the sentence that does the work here: nobody can guarantee a return, because nobody controls what the money earns. A promised figure is a claim about the promiser, not about the investment.

## The tells they share

- **Urgency.** The slot closes tonight, the batch is full, the promo ends at midnight. Time pressure exists to stop you checking.
- **A reward for recruiting.** If bringing a friend earns you money, the friend is the product.
- **Screenshots as proof.** A screenshot is a picture. It proves nothing about a business and takes minutes to fake.
- **A move somewhere private.** From a public page to a DM, from a DM to a personal number, from a company channel to a personal one.
- **Certainty about a number.** Guaranteed, risk free, fixed monthly return.
- **Somebody you love who already believes it.** The hard one, because the person recruiting you is not lying to you. They have been paid, and they do not know yet that they are also a victim.

Keep those six in mind, because the versions below are the same tells wearing different clothes.

## The shapes this takes for students, VAs and jobseekers

**The doubling group.** Investment, trading, an agricultural project, a lending pool, a foreign partner. The story changes and the engine does not. Early members are paid, they recruit sincerely because they believe it, and the collapse arrives without warning.

**The task scam.** A message offers easy work: like videos, rate hotel listings, complete "orders". The first small payments are real and land in your wallet on time. Then a bigger commission requires you to top up your own money to unlock a batch. Those small payments were not wages. They were the cost of buying your trust, and you are about to repay them with the rest.

**The job that charges you.** A recruiter offers online work: encoding, moderation, chat support. Before you can start there is a fee for a training kit, processing, a uniform or system access. Hold this rule flat: an employer pays you, you do not pay an employer. Money moving from you toward a job is the whole tell, whatever the fee is called.

**The OTP phish.** Someone calls, sounds like your bank or your wallet provider, and uses your name and maybe your last transaction. There is a problem with your account, they are fixing it, a code is coming, and they need you to read it back. A one-time code exists to prove that you are you. Reading it out is how the system gets told that the caller is you.

**The lending app whose real product is pressure.** It approves you in minutes, wants access to your contacts and photos before it releases anything, and starts messaging the people in your phone the moment a payment is late. The last lesson deals with what to do when you are already inside one.

Crypto has its own versions of all this, with mechanics that belong to that ground, and Basic Blockchain handles those. What you are learning here is the anatomy underneath them.

## The checks anyone can run

1. **Name the entity, then look it up at the source.** The SEC publishes advisories against groups soliciting investments without registration, and it publishes what is registered. Search there, not inside the group chat.
2. **Ask where the return comes from.** If the answer describes levels, referrals and recruitment rather than a business selling something, you have your answer.
3. **Verify through a channel you chose.** Hang up. Call the number printed on your card or on the provider's official page.
4. **Never pay to start work.** No deposits, no kits, no refundable fees, no exceptions.
5. **Give it a week.** A real opportunity survives a week of you thinking about it. The one that cannot has told you what it is.

## Before you answer the group chat

Take the last offer that reached your group chat and write one sentence naming where the money for the promised return would have to come from. If you cannot write that sentence, you have your answer. Send the same question back to whoever forwarded it.

lessons.title: Where your money sits
lessons.content_mdx:
# Where your money sits

Ask three people where their savings are and you get three answers: sa bank, nasa wallet ko, nandito lang sa bahay. Those are three different arrangements carrying three different risks, and knowing which one you are in changes what you do next.

## Cash at home

Nothing stands between you and the loss. Fire, flood, a break-in, a relative who knows about the tin, and the slow leak of a hundred pesos borrowed from yourself on a Tuesday. Cash at home also earns nothing while prices climb, which chapter 2 already covered: money doing nothing is quietly losing buying power.

Keeping a small amount at home for the day the power and the network are both out is sensible. Your emergency fund is not a shoebox.

## A bank deposit

When you deposit money in a bank, the bank owes it to you. Bank deposits here sit under a deposit insurance arrangement run by the PDIC, which covers deposits per depositor per bank, up to a limit fixed by law.

Two things follow from that shape. Coverage is per bank rather than per account, so three accounts in the same bank are still one exposure. And the limit is a number that has been changed by law before and can be changed again.

Do not trust a deposit insurance figure quoted in a group chat, on a tarpaulin, or in this lesson. There is no number here on purpose. Look it up on PDIC's own site on the day it matters to you.

Deposit insurance covers one thing: the bank failing. It does not cover you being talked into transferring money to a stranger, and it does not cover an investment product sold to you at a bank counter. If someone at a counter offers you something that pays more than a deposit, ask plainly whether it is a deposit or an investment, and ask for the answer in writing.

## E-wallets

An e-wallet is the app on your phone you use to send money, pay a bill, or receive a client payment. They are licensed to hold and move electronic money, and which one you use does not change any of the questions below.

Treat them as rails rather than vaults. They are built to move money, which is what they are good at. The protections attached to a balance sitting inside one are not automatically the same as a bank deposit's, and the arrangement differs by provider. Do not assume in either direction: ask your provider how your balance is held, and check the PDIC position at the source rather than trusting anyone's summary of it.

The behaviour that follows is simple. Money that has arrived and is not being spent this month should not live in the app you tap forty times a week.

## SSS and Pag-IBIG

Chapter 1 met these as lines on a payslip. They are also a place your money sits, and it is worth knowing which one. Contributing buys membership in arrangements that pay out under defined conditions, and freelancers and the self-employed can register and contribute on their own behalf rather than being left out of both.

Two habits are worth building. Check once a year that your contributions are posted under your own number, because a posting error found ten years later is a far worse problem than one found now. And take every figure, schedule and benefit rule from SSS and Pag-IBIG themselves, since those change and no course can hold them accurately.

## Keep the piles apart

Where money sits decides what happens to it. If your buffer, your spending money and the tax you owe are all in one account, you will spend the buffer without ever deciding to.

What works: one account you spend from, one place your buffer lives that is awkward enough to reach that you do not raid it for a sale, and, if you freelance, a separate holding place for money already promised to BIR and your contributions. Awkward is the feature. A buffer you can reach by tapping twice is not a buffer.

## The hygiene that makes theft harder

- **Your email password is the master key.** Whoever controls your email can reset almost everything else. Give it a password you use nowhere else.
- **Turn on the extra login step**, usually labelled two-factor authentication or a login code, wherever it is offered, on email first and money accounts second.
- **Never read a code to anyone.** Not to a caller who says they are from your bank, not to a buyer who wants to verify you, not to a friend messaging from an account that might not be theirs any more.
- **Your mobile number is part of the lock.** If you lose the SIM, report it to your provider quickly, because whoever holds it receives your codes.
- **Read your statements monthly.** A small unfamiliar charge is how a stolen card gets tested before the large one goes through.

## Try this

List every place money of yours is sitting right now: bank, wallet, cash at home, contributions, and anything lent to a friend. Next to each, write who carries the loss if it disappears tomorrow. That page is a truer picture of your finances than any budget.

lessons.title: The order to do things in
lessons.content_mdx:
# The order to do things in

Everything so far has been understanding. This lesson is sequence: what to do first when you are starting from behind, which is where plenty of people start.

One caveat before the sequence: this is a method, not a personalised plan, since nobody here knows your actual numbers.

## The sequence

**1. Name the numbers.** What comes in, what goes out, what you owe and to whom. Chapter 1 gave you the method. You cannot sequence anything until that list exists on paper.

**2. Build a first small buffer.** Not the full fund yet. Enough that the next flat tyre or fever does not become a new loan. This comes before attacking debt, because a payoff plan with nothing behind it collapses at the first surprise and you borrow again at a worse rate.

**3. Stop new borrowing.** This is the step people skip, and skipping it turns the rest into arithmetic with no ending. Take the borrowing apps off your phone. Paying down one balance while opening another is running on a treadmill.

**4. Kill the expensive debt.** List every balance with what it actually costs you over a year, using the method from chapter 2 rather than the headline rate. Then set each cost against the size of the balance behind it, because a big balance throws off a big figure without being the worse deal. A ₱5,000 balance costing ₱3,000 a year is costing you three fifths of itself. A ₱20,000 balance costing ₱4,000 a year is costing you a fifth. The smaller one is the worse deal. Pay the minimum on everything and aim everything spare at the biggest share. When that balance is gone, aim the same money at the next biggest share.

There is one honest exception. If your most expensive balance is so large that it will take a year to see it move, and you know from experience that you quit when nothing moves, clear a small balance first to prove to yourself the plan works, then go back to attacking by cost. Slightly more expensive and actually finished beats optimal and abandoned.

**5. Fill the fund.** Take the buffer up to a number sized against your own monthly spending, the way chapter 2 described.

**6. Then anything left can go to work.** Only here, and only once you can explain in your own words what you are putting money into and where its return comes from.

## When you cannot pay

Talk before the due date, not after. A lender you contacted first treats you differently from one that had to chase you, and asking about a restructured schedule is a normal request rather than a confession.

Keep records from the first missed payment: the amount you actually received, the amount you agreed to repay, every payment with its reference number, and every message they send. Pay through a traceable channel, never in cash to someone who turns up at your door.

Collection is a normal part of lending. Contacting your relatives to shame you is not collection, and neither is threatening you, posting about you, or messaging the people in your contact list. Screenshot everything with the date and the sender visible. Complaints about a lending or financing company go to the SEC, which is also where you check whether the lender is registered at all. Misuse of your personal data and your contact list goes to the National Privacy Commission. Banks and e-money providers have consumer assistance channels, and the BSP is where you look those up. Do not stop paying what you genuinely owe while a complaint is open, and do not pay a peso more because somebody frightened you into it.

## The monthly review

Fifteen minutes, the same day every month, phone on silent.

- What came in, and was it above or below the low month you budget from?
- Did the buffer move, up or down, and why?
- What is the balance on the debt you are attacking?
- One line: what is different next month?

That is the whole review. One you actually do every month beats a spreadsheet you abandon in March.

## Saying no without lying

Money leaves you through requests as much as through purchases. A cousin needs load, an ate needs to borrow until payday, a group is collecting for a gift.

You do not need a story. You need one sentence you can say twice without changing it: "Hindi ko kaya this month." Then stop talking. Explaining invites negotiation, and inventing a reason means having to remember it later.

If you are the one people come to, name in advance the amount you are willing to give each month, and decide inside that limit. Giving from a number you chose is generosity. Giving from whatever happens to be left is how a buffer disappears.

## What to take elsewhere

For anything about your specific money, the source beats a course: BIR for tax, SSS, PhilHealth and Pag-IBIG for contributions and benefits, PDIC for deposit insurance, the SEC for advisories and for checking whether an entity is registered.

If you consult a person, ask one question first: how do you get paid? Someone earning a commission on what you buy is a salesperson, which is not a scandal as long as you know it before you listen. Their answer tells you how to weigh everything that follows.

quiz.prompt: Jayson is offered online moderation work. The company has a website, an office address and sends him a contract. Before his first shift he must pay ₱1,500 for a training kit and system access, refundable after three months. What should he do?

options.text: Pay it and keep the receipt, since the amount is small next to the monthly salary being offered.
Check the company in SEC and DTI records first, then pay the fee if the registration comes back clean.
Treat the fee itself as the answer, keep his money, and carry on applying to employers that pay him.
Send half now and the rest after his first shift, so he loses less if the job turns out to be fake.

quiz.explanation: Money moves from an employer to you, never the other way, and the label on the fee does not change that. A registration record, a contract and an office address are all things a scheme can produce, so checking them cannot make a start-up fee acceptable. Paying half is still paying, and refundable after three months is a promise from the same people asking for the money.

quiz.prompt: Your Tita Baby has withdrawn twice from a lending pool that pays a fixed 20 percent a month. She is not lying: you have seen the money land in her account. She wants you in before the current batch closes on Friday. What is the sound response?

options.text: Join with an amount you could afford to lose, since your aunt has actually been paid and you do trust her.
Put in the smallest amount allowed as a test, withdraw it once, and only then decide about a bigger amount.
Wait a few months, watch whether her payouts keep arriving, and join later if the scheme is still running.
Ask where the return is generated, search the SEC advisories for the group, and put nothing in meanwhile.

quiz.explanation: Your aunt is evidence that early members get paid, which is how the mechanism works rather than proof that it is real: her payouts came from later members, and joining makes you one of them. A test amount funds somebody else's withdrawal and buys your trust with your own money. Waiting only means joining nearer the collapse. Ask where the money comes from and check the group at the SEC's own site.

quiz.prompt: A caller says she is from your bank's fraud team. She knows your name and your last transaction, says a transfer is being attempted right now, and needs the code arriving on your phone in order to block it. What do you do?

options.text: Read her the code, since she already knows your recent transaction and is trying to stop a theft in progress.
End the call, then ring the number printed on your card or on the bank's official page and ask there.
Ask for her employee number and branch first, then read the code once she has given you both of those.
Give her the code to stop the transfer, then change your password straight away as a precaution.

quiz.explanation: A one-time code exists to prove that you are you, so reading it out is how the system is told that the caller is you. Your name and a recent transaction can be phished or bought and are not identification. An employee number can be invented on the spot. Verify through a channel you chose, never the one that contacted you.

quiz.prompt: Cherry answers an ad for rating hotel listings. She is paid ₱90 twice, into her wallet, on time. Then the app says the next batch pays far more, but she must top up ₱1,500 of her own money to unlock it. What is happening, and what should she do?

options.text: The payments bought her trust, so she stops now, tops up nothing, and reports the account she dealt with.
The job is real but badly run, so she asks them to take the top-up out of the commission she has earned.
The risk is small next to the commission, so she tops up once and withdraws everything the moment it clears.
The system needs a deposit to release bigger batches, so she tops up the minimum and stops if nothing lands.

quiz.explanation: The two real payments were the cost of buying her trust, and the top-up is where they take them back along with the rest. Asking for it to be deducted sounds reasonable and gets refused with a new rule, because the deposit is the entire product. There is no batch behind the screen, so a plan to withdraw the moment it clears has nothing to wait for.

quiz.prompt: Elmer is three days late on a lending app. It has begun messaging people in his contacts calling him a scammer, and adding charges he does not recognise. He can pay the balance he actually agreed to. What is the best move?

options.text: Pay everything they are demanding today, added charges included, so the messages to his contacts stop at once.
Delete the app, change his number and wait it out, since they cannot reach him once he has gone quiet.
Screenshot every message, settle what he genuinely owes through a traceable channel, and report the conduct.
Borrow from a second app to clear the first one today, then deal with the new balance out of next month's pay.

quiz.explanation: The debt and the harassment are two separate problems and each needs its own action: pay what you owe through a channel that leaves a record, and document the conduct with dates and senders visible. Paying charges you do not recognise rewards the pressure and invites more. Going quiet leaves your contacts being messaged and the balance growing, and borrowing to repay a lender is how one app becomes three.

quiz.prompt: Grace owes three amounts: ₱4,000 on a lending app that charges her ₱1,000 a month, ₱6,000 from a 5-6 lender who wants ₱6,600 back over thirty days, and ₱10,000 to her uncle with no interest and no deadline. She has ₱1,000 spare this month. Where should it go?

options.text: The 5-6 loan, because the collector comes to the house daily and missing him carries the most immediate pressure.
The lending app, because its charge is the largest share of what she still owes there for each month it stays unpaid.
Her uncle, because family debt has a cost you cannot see on a statement and it protects a relationship she needs.
Split it evenly across the three, so every balance is moving down and none of the three lenders feels ignored.

quiz.explanation: Run it in pesos over a year first, the way chapter 2 taught. The app takes ₱1,000 a month, so ₱12,000 a year on a ₱4,000 balance. The 5-6 lender takes ₱600 a cycle, roughly twelve cycles, so about ₱7,200 a year on ₱6,000. Then set each cost against the balance behind it: a quarter of the app balance every month, against a tenth of the 5-6 balance. Both methods point at the app. The 5-6 balance is falling daily besides, which makes every peso still owed on it dearer than the headline suggests without ever closing that gap, and the daily collector feels more urgent, but urgency is not price. Her uncle costs nothing in pesos and belongs later. Splitting money evenly slows every payoff and finishes none of them.

quiz.prompt: Kim has finally saved three months of expenses. It sits in an envelope in her cabinet, and she has been dipping into it for sale items. Where should that money sit instead?

options.text: Left as cash at home, since it cannot be tapped away on a phone and no app can freeze her out of reaching it.
In the e-wallet she uses daily, so that in a real emergency the money is available to her within seconds.
In a scheme paying a fixed monthly return, since the money will be sitting there unused for months anyway.
In a deposit account she carries no card for, after checking at the source how deposits there are covered.

quiz.explanation: An emergency fund should be boring, reachable within days, and awkward enough that a sale does not qualify as an emergency. Cash at home is exposed to fire, theft and her own hand, and the wallet she taps daily is not separate from her spending at all. A fixed monthly return is a warning sign rather than a feature, and this is the last money that should be anywhere near one.

quiz.prompt: Ruby is a VA whose income moves. This month she is ₱3,000 ahead for the first time. She has no buffer, one lending app balance that costs her more than anything else she owes, and a cousin who has just asked to borrow. What should she do?

options.text: Set a small buffer aside, take the app off her phone, and put the rest of the money against that app balance.
Put the whole amount against the app balance, since it is the most expensive thing she owes by a clear margin.
Lend it to her cousin, because family asked first and a month this good is not something she can count on again.
Start investing it now, while she is ahead, so that a rare surplus is doing something rather than sitting idle.

quiz.explanation: Clearing an expensive balance with nothing behind it means the next fever or broken laptop goes straight back onto the same app, which is why a small buffer comes first and why the borrowing has to stop before any payoff can hold. Investing sits behind both a buffer and expensive debt. The cousin is a real decision, but one to make from an amount she named in advance, not from a rare surplus.

questions.prompt: The job offer said ₱23,000 a month. Your first payslip shows ₱20,410 landing in your account, and the deductions block lists four lines you have not read. You have already committed to about ₱21,000 of monthly spending. What do you do first?

options.text: Message HR that you have been shortchanged, since the offer letter said ₱23,000 and that is the figure the company agreed to put in your account.
Read the four deduction lines and name each one, then rebuild the whole budget on ₱20,410, because that is the only figure you can actually spend.
Keep the ₱21,000 plan running and cover the gap from savings, since a first payslip is often partial and the next one should land closer to the offer.
Ask a workmate what comes out of their payslip and copy the adjustment they made, since two people at the same employer are deducted in the same way.

questions.explanation: A job offer quotes gross pay. Mandatory contributions and withholding tax come out of it before anything reaches you, so ₱23,000 was never a number you could spend. Name each deduction line rather than treating the gap as one lump: you can only query a line you can identify, and some of those lines are contributions bought in your name rather than money lost. A workmate's payslip is not yours. Waiting for a better second payslip is how a monthly shortfall of a few hundred pesos turns into borrowing.

questions.prompt: You are a freelancer. A client's ₱45,000 payment lands on a Friday. Nothing was withheld from it: no tax, no contributions. Rent is due Monday. What is the right handling of that ₱45,000?

options.text: Treat the whole ₱45,000 as this month's income, pay Monday's rent out of it, and set aside for tax whatever survives to the end of the month.
Leave the ₱45,000 untouched until you know exactly what you owe, and run the whole month on whatever is left over from the client who paid you last.
Move the tax and contribution share out of the account the day it lands, then budget from what is left, because mixed money reads as spendable.
Assume the client withholds and remits your tax the way an employer would, and treat the ₱45,000 that arrived as money already cleared of it.

questions.explanation: Nothing withheld does not mean nothing owed. An employee never sees the contribution and tax money, which is the only reason it survives the month. The freelancer sees all of it, which is why it does not. Separating it the day it arrives is the whole fix, because one balance gives you no way to tell your money from money you are only holding. Some clients withhold and some do not, and either way it is not a thing to assume. What you owe, how to register and when to file are questions for the BIR or an accountant, not for this course.

questions.prompt: You tracked one real month. The surprises were ₱2,750 on food delivery across eleven orders, ₱1,900 on a phone plan you signed a two-year contract for, ₱850 on three subscriptions that renewed on their own, and ₱600 of load top-ups. You want next month to come out different. Where do you look first?

options.text: The delivery orders and the top-ups, after one sitting spent cancelling the subscriptions, since those two get decided again every day.
The phone plan, since ₱1,900 is the largest single line in that list and going after the biggest number is what changes a month fastest.
The subscriptions and nothing else, since the ₱850 is the only money on that list that leaves you without any decision at all.
The phone plan and the subscriptions together, since anything that renews or runs on a contract is the part of a budget you can control.

questions.explanation: Fixed costs were decided once and are not available to be decided again this month: a two-year contract is locked, whatever its size. Variable costs come back up for a decision every day, which is where a month is won or lost. Cancel the silent renewals by all means, and it takes one sitting, but that is one decision that then returns nothing further, and it is not the only money on the list leaving without a decision: eleven delivery orders and a string of small top-ups are decisions you barely register making. Eleven orders is eleven chances to choose differently. The phone plan is the largest line and the least available to you, which is what makes going after the biggest number the wrong instinct here.

questions.prompt: You freelance. A fat month leaves ₱30,000 sitting in the holding account your client payments land in, on top of the salary you already paid yourself on the fifth. A client then agrees to a higher rate starting next month. What changes about the amount you pay yourself on the fifth?

options.text: Raise it now to match the new rate, since a client agreeing to pay more is exactly the evidence that your old salary figure was set too low.
Raise it by the ₱30,000 spread over the next few months, so the surplus reaches you instead of sitting in an account you never spend from.
Pay yourself the whole ₱30,000 this month and go back to the usual figure after, since the money is already earned and it is already yours.
Nothing yet. Your salary moves when the thin months move, so the ₱30,000 stays put and the new rate has to show up in a low month first.

questions.explanation: The holding account exists so that the date and the amount of your own pay are boring. A fat month refills it, a thin month draws it down, and that only works if the salary itself stops moving every time a good month lands. One client agreeing a higher rate is a promise about next month, not a new low month, so the figure to watch is still what arrives when the work is thin. Raising your pay on the strength of ₱30,000 you have not needed yet is how a surplus quietly turns into a fixed cost. Paying the whole surplus out this month is the same mistake in one go: it empties the thing that pays you in the next quiet month. Raise your own pay when the low month itself rises, and not before.

questions.prompt: It is a thin month and you are ₱3,000 short of ₱7,500 rent due in four days. A lending app will approve ₱3,000 today, with a ₱450 fee taken off the top and the full ₱3,000 due back in fourteen days. What do you do?

options.text: Pay the ₱4,500 you already have and tell the landlord the rest follows when you are next paid, without naming a date for it while the month is uncertain.
Talk to the landlord today about splitting this month's rent in two, because a conversation held before you are late costs nothing and stays out of next month.
Borrow ₱3,450 from the app so that ₱3,000 still reaches you once the ₱450 is taken off the top, then repay the whole of it out of next month's income.
Take the loan and use the fourteen-day deadline as pressure to find extra work, since a fixed date turns a vague plan to earn more into something you act on.

questions.explanation: Read the offer properly first. The fee comes off the top, so ₱3,000 borrowed puts ₱2,550 in your hand and you are still short of the rent. That is what any deduction before the money reaches you does to an offer. Then price it: ₱450 to use ₱2,550 for two weeks. Work out what that same charge comes to if you repeat it through a year and you will see its real size. Paying part and leaving the rest open is not the same as agreeing terms, because an amount and a date said out loud are what a landlord can plan around, and silence about the date is what turns a short month into a demand letter. Nothing about the loan makes next month easier either, since the shortfall returns with a repayment on top of it. What changes the month is a conversation held before you are late, which costs nothing.

questions.prompt: You have ₱20,000 spare. You also carry a ₱20,000 card balance that costs you about ₱600 a month while it sits there, and you have no buffer at all. A colleague says to get the ₱20,000 invested before inflation eats it. What is the sound sequence?

options.text: Hold back a small starter buffer, put the rest of it against the card, then rebuild the fund with the ₱600 a month you are no longer paying out.
Invest it and keep servicing the card each month, since a return compounding over years beats a monthly cost you can already afford to carry.
Split it: ₱10,000 invested and ₱10,000 against the card, so both jobs move at once and neither one has to sit and wait for the other to finish.
Build the entire emergency fund out of it first and leave the card alone until that is done, since the buffer comes before everything else in the order.

questions.explanation: Killing a cost you are certainly paying is the one return nobody has to promise you: the ₱600 a month stops, for certain, the day the balance does. No investment can offer that, and one that claims to is describing something impossible. The buffer rule is not a ritual, though. It exists so the next surprise does not go straight back onto the card, and a small starter amount does that job while the expensive balance dies. Building the full fund first leaves the card charging you for months, and splitting the money does the same at half speed. What to invest in afterwards is not something this course answers: that is a question for a licensed professional, and the first thing to ask one is how they get paid.

questions.prompt: Your buffer is at ₱18,000. Three things land in the same week. Your sister's enrollment, ₱6,000, on a date the school published in June. A phone that still works but has gone slow, ₱9,000 to replace. And your father admitted overnight, ₱7,000. Which of them is the buffer for?

options.text: The admission and the enrollment, because both are family obligations you cannot refuse and neither of them can be pushed into a later month.
The phone only. It is the thing you work on, and a tool you earn with is the case a buffer exists for, even when the old one still switches on.
The admission only. It was not planned, it will not wait, and not dealing with it costs more than dealing with it. The other two fail a test.
All three. The week is the emergency, and a buffer that cannot cover the week you are actually having is not doing very much for you at all.

questions.explanation: Three tests, and a cost has to pass all of them: it was not planned, it will not wait, and not dealing with it costs more than dealing with it. The admission passes all three. The enrollment fails the first one, because a date published in June is a budget line you should have been setting aside for monthly, and paying for it out of the buffer is how a known cost gets dressed up as a shock. A phone that still works fails the second and the third. Slow is an expense with a date on it, not an emergency, and a tool you earn with only becomes urgent when it stops. Being a family obligation is not one of the tests. Write your own version of this list before you need it, because the moment you need it everything on the week feels urgent.

questions.prompt: Noel needs ₱21,000 to rebuild his tricycle's engine before the fiesta rush, repaid over seven months at ₱3,000 of principal each month. Lender X charges 2.5% a month on the original ₱21,000 for all seven months, no fees. Lender Y charges 3.5% a month on what he still owes, plus a ₱400 processing fee taken off the top. Which offer costs him less?

options.text: Lender X, because 2.5% a month is lower than 3.5% a month and X charges no processing fee at all, so X wins on both halves of the price.
Lender X, because Y's charge still starts on the whole ₱21,000 in the first month, and Y then adds a fee that X does not charge him at all.
Take whichever lender releases the money first, since both charges are small next to being short of the ₱21,000, and speed is the part he can feel.
Lender Y: X's 2.5% keeps hitting the original ₱21,000 every month while he pays it down, so X totals ₱3,675 against Y's ₱3,340 with the fee.

questions.explanation: Turn both into pesos over the life of the loan. X: 2.5% of ₱21,000 is ₱525 a month, seven times over, ₱3,675, and Noel is still paying ₱525 in the final month when he only owes ₱3,000. Y: his balance falls ₱21,000, ₱18,000, ₱15,000, ₱12,000, ₱9,000, ₱6,000, ₱3,000 across the seven months, and those add up to ₱84,000, so 3.5% of that is ₱2,940. Add the ₱400 fee and Y totals ₱3,340. That is the same sum chapter 2 runs on Vince, on a different shape of loan. The higher headline rate costs less here because it is charged on what Noel still owes. A rate on the original amount and a rate on the balance are different products, which is why the two percentages alone tell you nothing, and why taking whichever money arrives first is a decision made on speed rather than on price.

questions.prompt: A vendor you know borrows ₱6,000 from a 5-6 lender and pays back ₱7,200 in daily instalments over forty days. She says it is fine, it is only ₱1,200, and she has never missed a day. You are thinking of funding your own stall restock the same way. How do you size that offer honestly?

options.text: It is ₱1,200 on ₱6,000, so the cost is a fifth of what you borrowed, and that fifth is the figure to hold up against any other lender's offer.
Work out the cost of funding every restock that way through a year: roughly nine cycles turns that ₱1,200 into ₱10,800 on the same ₱6,000.
Compare it on the daily payment. Around ₱180 a day out of stall takings is small and predictable, and a payment you can meet daily is affordable.
Judge it on her record. A lender who has never had to chase her is pricing convenience rather than risk, so the charge is not really interest at all.

questions.explanation: Any borrowing becomes comparable once you turn it into what leaves your pocket over the same stretch of time, and a year is the stretch that makes offers line up. Forty days is roughly a ninth of a year, so a stall funded this way all year pays that ₱1,200 about nine times over on the same ₱6,000. A cost quoted per cycle or per day hides its size precisely because the period is short. Whether you can meet the daily payment is a different question from what the money costs, and the ease of that daily payment is what makes the arrangement so easy to keep using.

questions.prompt: Someone from your old BPO team has been paid a fixed ₱4,000 a week for three months by a pool his neighbour runs, and he has the transfer screenshots. He has withdrawn twice. He wants you in with ₱20,000 and says the money is made buying and reselling secondhand phones. What is the correct read?

options.text: Three months of payouts is evidence it works, so a small ₱5,000 test is a reasonable way to see for yourself before you put in anything larger.
Reselling phones is a real trade and can pay that well in a good month, so the live question is his neighbour's margin, and three months speaks to it.
Nobody can promise a fixed weekly return on a trade they do not control, and the early payouts are what a scheme spends to bring in the next batch.
Say no, and tell him his neighbour is running a criminal operation, so that he pulls his own money out before the whole thing collapses under him.

questions.explanation: A return comes out of an outcome nobody controls, so a fixed weekly figure is not a forecast. It is a promise about something the promiser cannot deliver, and that alone settles it. Your workmate is not lying about the payouts: he was paid, out of money later members put in, which is why the early ones get paid and get seen. A test amount funds somebody else's withdrawal and buys your trust with your own money. A real margin on secondhand phones would move week to week the way every trade does, so a fixed weekly figure is the tell rather than the attraction. The checks you can actually run sit at the source: whether the entity is registered with the SEC, and whether the SEC has published an advisory about it. Refusing is right. Calling his neighbour a criminal ends the conversation, and he is the one with money still inside.

questions.prompt: A group in your chat calls itself a capital build-up circle. It pays members a fixed weekly amount and says the money is made reselling rice in bulk. It has a business name certificate, an office in a mall, a written contract, and four members who will tell you they have been paid. You have ₱15,000 and until Friday. Which check actually tells you something?

options.text: Search the SEC for whether the entity may take money from the public and for any advisory against it, then give the decision a week before you answer.
Visit the office and read the contract in full, since a group with a lease and a signed document has far more to lose than an anonymous chat thread does.
Ask the four paid members how long they have been in and how much they have taken out, since a payout record over time is the hardest thing to fake.
Check the business name certificate against the DTI register, since a name registered to real people is what you would need in order to file a case.

questions.explanation: Only one of those four looks at whether the group is allowed to take money from the public at all, and it is run at the source rather than inside the group. The SEC publishes what is registered and publishes advisories against groups soliciting investments without it, so that is the search worth running. The other three test things a scheme can produce cheaply. An office and a contract cost a month of rent and an afternoon. A business name certificate says a name exists, not that its holder may sell you an investment. And the four paid members are the mechanism rather than evidence against it: early members are paid out of what later members put in, which is exactly why you are being shown them. Then give it a week. A real opportunity survives a week of you thinking about it, and the Friday deadline is there to stop you checking.

questions.prompt: Your phone is snatched on a jeep. The SIM inside it receives the login codes for your bank, your e-wallet and two client platforms. Your email opens on that phone without a password. You reach a laptop twenty minutes later. What do you do first?

options.text: Change the bank and e-wallet passwords first and get to the email later, since the money is what is at risk and an inbox holds nothing anyone can spend.
File a police blotter first and send it to the bank, so that anything spent from tonight onward is covered by a report you made before it happened.
Wait for a replacement SIM before changing anything, since a password change now sends its confirmation code to a phone somebody else is holding.
Get the provider to block the SIM and change the email password before anything else, because one of them receives your codes and the other resets the rest.

questions.explanation: Whoever controls your email can reset almost everything else, which is why it carries a password you use nowhere else and why it cannot wait. Your mobile number is the other half of the same lock: whoever holds the SIM receives your codes, so blocking it with the provider is tonight's job rather than tomorrow's errand. Going for the money accounts first leaves someone able to undo every change you just made, through a reset link sent to the inbox you left open. A blotter is worth having and stops nothing from leaving tonight. And waiting for a replacement SIM has it backwards: it is precisely because the codes are reaching somebody else that you cut the SIM off now. Read a code to nobody afterwards, whatever they say they are calling about.

questions.prompt: You have finished a ₱60,000 emergency fund. It is sitting in the e-wallet you use every day for food and fares. One friend says move it to a bank deposit because of PDIC. Another says keep it as cash at home so that nothing can freeze it. How do you decide?

options.text: Leave it in the wallet. It is the fastest money to reach in an emergency, and same-day reach is the whole purpose of a fund like this one.
Move it somewhere boring to reach and covered by deposit insurance, checking the current limit and what your provider holds at the source.
Split it three ways across the wallet, the bank and cash at home, so that no single failure or freeze can take the entire fund away from you.
Keep it as cash at home. Money in your hand cannot be frozen, locked out by a system outage, or taken by whoever gets into one of your accounts.

questions.explanation: Two questions decide where a fund sits: who carries the risk if the holder fails, and how easily you can spend it by accident. The wallet you pay fares from fails the second question badly. An e-wallet is a payment rail rather than a vault, so whether a balance there sits inside an insured bank deposit is something to ask the provider directly. Bank deposits sit under the PDIC arrangement, which insures a depositor per bank up to a limit fixed by law. Check that limit at PDIC itself rather than trusting a figure quoted anywhere, including in this course, because it is set by law and can be changed. Cash at home has no insurer and no friction at all.

questions.prompt: Ligaya lists four debts: ₱15,000 on a credit card that costs her about ₱3,750 a year to carry, ₱5,000 owed to a lending app that costs her about ₱2,500 a year, ₱8,000 owed through a coworker's informal lending circle that costs her about ₱2,880 a year, and ₱30,000 borrowed from her Ate Baby, who charges nothing and has never named a date. She can put ₱2,500 a month at one of them.

options.text: The lending app: it costs the most for its size and it is the smallest of the three priced debts, so no new borrowing starts anywhere while she works it down.
Ate Baby, because a debt to family is paid in the relationship rather than in pesos, and that is the more expensive thing to be slowly losing.
The card, since ₱3,750 a year is the largest amount leaving her pocket of the four, and the biggest cost is the one to kill ahead of the rest.
Split the ₱2,500 across all four, so every balance is moving and no lender has a reason to start chasing her or adding a penalty on top.

questions.explanation: Cost on its own is the wrong comparison, because a bigger balance throws off a bigger figure without being the worse deal. Set each cost against the balance behind it: the app is ₱2,500 on ₱5,000, half the balance every year. The coworker's circle is ₱2,880 on ₱8,000, a little over a third. The card is ₱3,750 on ₱15,000, a quarter. The app is the worst deal by a clear margin, and it is also the smallest balance, so it is the one that can actually finish. When it ends, the ₱2,500 and the money it was eating both move to whichever priced debt is next. Ate Baby is owed real money and deserves a real conversation about a timeline, but paying her first buys nothing while three priced debts keep running. None of this works at all if new borrowing continues anywhere while Ligaya is doing it, which is why stopping that comes before the ordering, and splitting the money across all four slows every payoff and finishes none of them.

questions.prompt: You are eleven days late on a ₱4,000 loan from an app. It has messaged four people in your contacts, including a former employer, calling you a scammer. It now wants the full balance plus penalties today. You have ₱1,500 you could pay right now.

options.text: Screenshot every message and report them, then hold the ₱1,500 back until a regulator has ruled on the charges you never agreed to.
Pay the whole thing today with a loan from a second app, because the messages will only reach further while any balance is still outstanding.
Pay the ₱1,500 today through a channel that leaves a record, tell them in writing when the rest follows, and keep every message as evidence.
Reply telling them to stop, that contacting your employer is illegal, and that you will take them to court if another one of your contacts is messaged.

questions.explanation: Two things are true at once and you act on both. The money is genuinely owed, so paying what you can through a traceable channel and saying in writing when the rest follows is the right move on the debt. Shaming you through your contact list is a separate matter: that is conduct, you document it, and screenshots taken today are the only record you will control. A lending company answers to the SEC, and harvesting your contacts to pressure you is a matter for the National Privacy Commission. Reporting and then holding the money back is the near miss: a complaint takes time, the balance grows while it runs, and you do not stop paying what you genuinely owe while one is open. Borrowing from a second app to clear the first is how one debt becomes two on the same day, and a threat to sue is only talk to people betting you are too embarrassed to tell anybody.
